newsitem.title: UK: British shares fall sharply as jitters resurface.
newsitem.headline: British shares fall sharply as jitters resurface.

text.p: Renewed fears of a fresh shakeout on Wall Street sent British shares sharply lower on Wednesday, just three trading days after the market suffered its biggest percentage loss in over two years.

Taking its lead from tumbling Asian markets, the FTSE 100 index fell over 50 points at one stage, wiping some 8.5 billion pounds ($14.09 billion) off its value, though by 1120 GMT it had rallied to be down 41.0 points at 3,994.7.
Traders said no single factor had sparked the losses, though current jittery markets did not need much excuse to turn tail from their recovery of the past two sessions.
Some said losses in Standard & Poor's 500 index futures during Far Eastern trading had sparked the latest bout of jitters, flagging a sharply weaker opening on Wall Street.

Traders also blamed rumours that a major U.S. corporation was about to issue a profit warning for the upheaval, while others pointed to a Wall Street Journal report that Japanese investors may slow their purchases of U.S. government bonds.
Either way, London equities were left reeling after barely catching their breath from last Friday's fall, when the FTSE at one stage dropped to its lowest level for three months.

"This time it's a lot more worrying," said one senior trader in London. "People expect a one-off hit occasionally, but for it to crack again so soon, people will think there really is a serious problem in the markets."
"It could be longer-lasting this time," he said.

Today's tumble came after Alan Greenspan, head of the Fed (U.S. central bank), last week spooked world markets with remarks on the "irrational exuberance" of the markets. The subsequent global shake-out has been dubbed "grey Friday".

Investors were also nervous ahead of the November U.S. producer price report due at 1330 GMT today. The data is expected to show a rise of 0.3 percent, but faster growth would raise fears that interest rates might rise.
Many London traders and investment strategists have argued for some time that the U.S. markets were overvalued after their strong rise this year.
And though the London stock market has underperformed compared with the U.S., it remains prey to influences from the world's biggest economy.
British blue chips have risen around nine percent so far this year while the Dow has raced up nearly 30 percent, raising fears that a substantial correction cannot be too far away.
Greenspan's comments were enough to bring those fears of a correction to the surface.

No rise in U.S. interest rates is expected in the near term yet the Fed chief's comments were taken as a signal that he would tighten credit if he thought a dangerous "bubble" was developing in the markets. ($1=.6034 Pound)
